newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban deny rounding up political foes.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban deny rounding up political foes.

text.p: Afghanistan's Islamist Taleban rulers, responding to accusations of human rights abuses, denied on Thursday that they had been rounding up members of the ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani in Kabul.

"There have been no arrests for political crimes," acting Information and Culture Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told the official Bakhtar news agency. "We are only interrogating those involved in looting in the Taleban's name."
He said fewer than 70 people had been detained. "These people will be put on trial on the basis of Islamic Sharia law," Bakhtar quoted him as saying.

The London-based human rights group Amnesty International accused the Taleban on Wednesday of seizing up to 1,000 prisoners in house-to-house searches in the capital in what it called a reign of terror.

Residents in the diplomatic Wazir Akbar Khan area said Taleban fighters had been taking over houses previously occupied by former government commanders and politicians, but could not say if any arrests had been made.
Mutaqi hit back at critics of the Taleban drive to impose a strict Islamic order on Afghanistan, saying they were meddling in Afghan affairs.

"The Moslem people of Afghanistan want implementation of Islamic Sharia," he said. "Propaganda by some international circles about the system of running the country is considered interference in the internal affairs of Afghanistan, which contradicts international humanitarian ethics."
The Taleban have begun to tighten up on the foreign media in Kabul and at frontlines north of the city, trying to prevent photographers and cameramen from covering military activity.
Mutaqi was quoted as saying that "military installations" shout not be photographed, adding that Islam forbids photographing human beings.
The Taleban's leader and founder, Mullah Mohammad Omar, made another appeal on Thursday for international recognition.

In a decree published in the Taleban newspaper Shariat one week after the Islamic warriors ousted the government of former president Burhanuddin Rabbani, Omar asked the world to recognise the new administration in Kabul and urged its estimated one million people to stay in the city.

"All ambassadors to foreign countries are suspended and have no authority to work," said Omar, who is based in the southern city of Kandahar. "Different countries of the world are duty-bound to protect Afghanistan's properties abroad and no ambassador has the right to cash cheques.
"The people of Kabul are requested not to leave the city. Those who have left already may return and their security will be assured," Omar said.

Witnesses said hundreds of people had been crowding the capital's main bus station at Pul-i-Mahmood Khan in the past few days, heading down the highway to the eastern city of Jalalabad en route to neighbouring Pakistan.
The Taleban have told women government employees to stay at home on full pay until workplaces can be reorganised to separate men and women.
Kabul Radio exhorted people to pray five times a day at their local mosque, but did not say what would happen to those who failed to conform.
The Taleban movement have stamped their seal on Kabul with edicts reflecting its purist vision of Islamic behaviour.

In the process it has aroused growing international concern about its attitude to human rights, particularly those of women, who the Taleban say must be segregated from men in virtually every activity outside the home.

Already holding about three-quarters of Afghanistan's 33 provinces, the Taleban have been preparing to push former government forces led by Ahmed Shah Masood out of their Panjsher Valley redoubt northeast of Kabul.
Reuter photographer Patrick de Noirmont said the front line at the entrance to the rugged valley was calm on Thursday.
The Taleban's military drive to extend their control over Afghanistan has provoked alarm among its northern neighbours.
Russia has called a summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States starting in the Kazakh capital Almaty on Friday to discuss the Taleban's rise to power.
